english: Is it okay to talk (on the phone) right now?
usage: Is now a good time to talk?
the standard polite opener AFTER you placed the call and they picked up
Are you free to talk right now?
지금 = right now; pins the timing so they know you mean this moment
Do you have a minute to talk?
잠깐 (briefly) shrinks the ask and makes it easy to say yes
반말 해체; only with close friends/younger people
examples: A: 여보세요, 김 과장님? 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? / B: 네, 말씀하세요.
A: Hello, Manager Kim? Is now a good time to talk? / B: Yes, go ahead.
model call opener — 여보세요 first, then the check; B's 말씀하세요 signals the green light
바쁘신데 죄송해요. 잠깐 통화 괜찮으세요?
Sorry to bother you when you're busy. Do you have a minute?
lead with 죄송해요 before the request to soften any imposition
야, 통화 괜찮아? 할 말 있어.
Hey, can you talk? I've got something to say.
반말 between close friends; -세요 disappears entirely in this register
nuance: This is the reflexive courtesy line the CALLER says the instant the other person answers — you confirm they can actually talk before diving in, the way an English speaker says 'Is this a good time?' The literal structure is 통화 ('a phone conversation') + 괜찮으세요? ('is it okay for you?'), so you're asking whether a call is okay for THEM. 통화(通話) is Sino-Korean, 通 'pass/connect' + 話 'speech,' meaning a connected voice conversation — it is strictly phone or voice-call territory; for face-to-face talking use 얘기 or 대화. The honorific 괜찮으세요? must stay with any boss, elder, or client. Key 변형형: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? (adds 지금 to pin the moment), 잠깐 통화 괜찮으세요? (adds 잠깐 to minimize the ask), and bare 괜찮아? in 반말. A near-synonym is 지금 시간 괜찮으세요? ('do you have time now?'), but that works in any context (in person, over text), while 통화 괜찮으세요? anchors you specifically to this live call. The big English-speaker directional trap: only the CALLER asks this — the person who PICKED UP does not confirm permission; they simply respond 네, 말씀하세요 or 잠깐만요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '통화(call) + 괜찮으세요?(is it okay for you)?' — asking whether a connected conversation is acceptable RIGHT NOW. The caller says it; the receiver does not. It is the Korean equivalent of 'Is this a good time?'

Said the moment the other person picks up, before any content. -세요 (존댓말) is mandatory with bosses, elders, clients, and anyone you'd 존댓말. Flip to 괜찮아? only with close friends or younger people you speak to in 반말.

지금 시간 괜찮으세요? is the closest rival — it asks 'do you have time?' and works in any medium (in person, text, call). 통화 괜찮으세요? is phone-exclusive; it explicitly names the call as the thing you're asking permission for.
지금 통화 괜찮으세요? (adds 지금 to pin the moment) → 잠깐 통화 괜찮으세요? (adds 잠깐 to minimize the ask) → 통화 괜찮으세요? (baseline) → 통화 괜찮아? (반말). The honorific ending -세요 on 괜찮다 is formed as 괜찮- + -으시- + -어요 → 괜찮으세요.

Direction error: English speakers sometimes say it after ANSWERING a call ('Hello, is now a good time?'). Only the dialer asks this; the receiver simply responds. A second trap: using 괜찮아? with a senior colleague — always 괜찮으세요? with any 존댓말 relationship.

mistakes: Asking it when YOU received the call. The caller initiates this check; if you answered, you just say 네, 여보세요? — the dialer is the one who confirms it's a good time.
Using 괜찮아? with a boss or client. It is 반말 and sounds too familiar with anyone you'd 존댓말 — the honorific 괜찮으세요? (괜찮- + 으시- + 어요) is the safe default.
Saying 통화 to mean an in-person chat. 통화 is strictly a phone call; a face-to-face conversation is 대화 or just 얘기 — '얘기 좀 괜찮아요?' for talking in person.

english: Please hold (don't hang up), and wait a moment
usage: Please don't hang up and hold on
full polite form said to a caller you've put on hold
Please stay on the line for a moment
끊지 마시고 inserts honorific -시-; the extra-polite call-center grade
shorter and brisk; 잠깐만요 = 'just a sec'
반말 to a friend; note 주세요 is gone
examples: A: 담당자 연결 부탁드려요. / B: 네, 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요. 바로 연결해 드릴게요.
A: Could you connect me to the right person? / B: Of course, please hold — I'll put you right through.
full service exchange: caller's request, agent's hold phrase, then transfer promise
담당자 확인해 드릴게요. 끊지 마시고 잠시만 기다려 주세요.
I'll check with the person in charge. Please stay on the line a moment.
call-center grade; 마시고 carries the honorific -시-; 잠시만 adds urgency
엄마한테 물어볼게. 끊지 말고 기다려.
I'll ask Mom. Don't hang up, hold on.
casual household hand-off; no 주세요, plain 기다려
nuance: This phrase is what the person holding the receiver says when they must step away briefly but want you to remain on the line — the Korean equivalent of 'please hold.' Two clauses are bolted together: 끊지 말고 ('don't hang up and instead') warns you off ending the call, while 기다려 주세요 ('please wait for me') uses the favor verb 주다 to frame the wait as a kindness you're granting. 끊다 literally means 'to cut or sever,' which is exactly how Korean conceptualizes hanging up — you cut the call. Without 주세요, bare 기다려 sounds like a command; bare 끊지 마 sounds curt to a customer. The critical confusion to avoid is 끊다 (end a call) vs 끄다 (power off a device): a phone call is 끊어, but a TV, light, or powered device is 꺼. A near-synonym hold phrase is 잠시만 기다려 주세요 ('please wait a moment'), which only asks you to wait; 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 adds the explicit 'don't hang up,' making it the right choice when there's any risk the caller gives up and disconnects.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'don't cut (끊지 말고) + please wait for me (기다려 주세요).' Said by whoever is on the line when they need to step away briefly. The two clauses together equal the English 'please hold.' The favor verb 주다 softens the wait into a polite request, not a command.

Used in service contexts (call centers, offices) and at home. Keep 주세요 with any stranger or customer. 끊지 마시고 기다려 주세요 (with -시-) is the extra-polite call-center standard. Drop to 끊지 말고 기다려 only with intimates.

잠시만 기다려 주세요 ('please wait a moment') only asks you to wait and says nothing about hanging up. 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 explicitly warns 'don't hang up' — use it whenever the hold is long enough that the caller might give up.
끊지 마시고 잠시만 기다려 주세요 (extra-polite, -시-) → 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 (standard) → 끊지 말고 잠깐만요 (quick/brisk) → 끊지 말고 기다려 (반말). The honorific -시- in 마시고 marks the formal tier.

Confusing 끊다 (end a call) with 끄다 (power off): '전화 끊어' = hang up the phone; '불 꺼' = turn off the light; '전화 꺼' = power off the phone itself. These are different actions. Also: dropping 주세요 with a customer turns a request into an order.

mistakes: Confusing 끊다 with 끄다. A phone call is hung up: 전화 끊어; a device is turned off: 불 꺼 / 휴대폰 꺼. Saying 전화 꺼 means 'turn the phone OFF,' a different action.
Dropping 주세요 with a customer. 끊지 말고 기다려 to a stranger sounds like an order; the favor verb 기다려 주세요 makes it a polite request.
Writing 끊지 as 끈지. The verb is 끊다 (with the ㄶ cluster); 끈 means 'a string,' so 끈지 말고 is a spelling slip.

english: Shall I take a message (for them)?
usage: Would you like me to leave a message?
humble offer to write down a message for the absent person
Is there anything you'd like me to pass on?
Would you like to leave a message?
-시겠어요 puts the choice politely on the caller
Want me to leave them a message?
examples: A: 김 부장님 좀 바꿔 주세요. / B: 자리에 안 계신데요. 메모 남겨 드릴까요?
A: Could I speak to Manager Kim? / B: He's not at his desk right now — shall I take a message?
realistic call exchange: request → absence explanation → message offer; B uses 안 계신데요 to honor Kim
회의 중이신데, 메모 남겨 드릴까요?
They're in a meeting — would you like to leave a message?
-신데 = honorific soft lead-in providing the reason before the offer
형 지금 없는데, 메모 남겨 줄까?
Bro's not here — want me to pass on a message?
casual at home; 줄까 instead of 드릴까요; 형 = older brother
nuance: Said by whoever answers when the person the caller wants is unavailable, offering to write the caller's message down for the absent party. The engine is 드리다, the humble verb meaning 'to give / do for' a person you respect, so 남겨 드릴까요? politely volunteers to take a note as a favor to you — compare 남겨 줄까? (with plain 주다), the casual home version. 메모 here is borrowed from English 'memo' but in Korean refers specifically to a short handwritten or jotted note, not a formal corporate circular. A near-synonym phrase is 전하실 말씀 있으세요? ('is there anything to convey?'), which is slightly more formal and avoids the English loanword 메모 entirely, making it the safer choice in ultra-formal or governmental settings. The verb 남기다 ('leave behind') trips learners conjugating it: 남기- + -어 contracts neatly to 남겨, not 남기어 or 남겨다. Register is the central pitfall: offering 남겨 줄까요? to a business caller uses plain 주다 where humble 드리다 is expected, because you are doing the favor for both the caller AND the absent colleague.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '남겨(leave) + 드릴까요?(shall I do for you?)' — a humble offer to take a note for the absent person. The humble 드리다 (not plain 주다) signals you are performing the favor upward, towards the caller and the absent person simultaneously.

Said at a reception desk, in an office, or over the phone when the wanted person is away. With customers or seniors, 드릴까요 is mandatory. At home or with close peers, 줄까? is fine. 전하실 말씀 있으세요? is the ultra-formal alternative for official or governmental contexts.

메시지 남기시겠어요? ('would you like to leave a message?') puts the initiative on the CALLER — they choose to leave it. 메모 남겨 드릴까요? puts the initiative on YOU — you volunteer to take it. 전하실 말씀 있으세요? avoids the loanword 메모 and is more formal.
남기다 → 남겨 → 남겨 드릴까요? (humble offer) / 남겨 줄까? (반말). The contraction 남기어 → 남겨 is regular for -이어 verbs.

Offering 남겨 줄까요? to a customer swaps humble 드리다 for plain 주다, which undercuts the politeness needed in a service setting. Also: treating 메모 as a 'corporate memo' — in Korean everyday speech, 메모 is just a quick note or jot, not a formal document.

mistakes: Using 남겨 줄까요? to a customer. The situation calls for the humble 드리다: 남겨 드릴까요?. Plain 주다 (줄까요) is fine at home but under-polite at a reception desk.
Writing 남기다 as 남끼다. The stem is 남기- (남겨 = 남기 + 어). 남끼다 is not a word.
Treating 메모 like an English 'memo' (a formal circular). On the phone 메모 = a quick message/note; the office document is 공지 or 회람, not 메모.

usage: agent transferring your call to another line — humble -아 드릴게요
I'll connect you to the right department
담당 부서 = 'department in charge'; -로 marks the destination
formal -겠습니다 grade heard in call centers
반말, e.g. patching a friend through
examples: A: 고객센터 어디로 연결해 줘요? / B: 기술 지원팀으로 연결해 드릴게요. 잠시만요.
A: Which department should I go to? / B: I'll connect you to tech support. One moment.
A/B transfer request and response; -팀으로 marks the target
제가 처리할 수 없는 건이라, 담당자에게 연결해 드릴게요.
I can't handle this, so I'll transfer you to the right person.
-이라 gives the reason for escalating the call
아, 그건 누나가 알아. 연결해 줄게.
Oh, my sister knows that. I'll put her on.
casual hand-off at home; plain 줄게, not 드릴게요
nuance: This is the agent's phrase for transferring a caller to another extension or department — you are routing the CALL through the system to a new endpoint. 연결(連結) is Sino-Korean: 連 'join' + 結 'tie,' literally 'join-and-bind,' which captures a technical connection between two telephone lines. The humble -아 드리다 frames the routing as a favor done for the caller, which is why formal centers escalate to 연결해 드리겠습니다. The most important near-synonym contrast is 연결 vs 바꾸다: 연결해 드릴게요 means routing the call through a phone system to a new line or department (you may not even see the person), while 바꿔 드릴게요 means handing the same physical handset to a person who is standing right there — two completely different mechanical acts. A second critical contrast is 연결 vs 연락: 연결 = connect two parties right now; 연락 = reach out to someone later. Saying 나중에 연결드릴게요 to mean 'I'll contact you later' is a wiring error. Key 변형형: 연결해 드릴게요 (standard) → 연결해 드리겠습니다 (extra-formal) → 연결해 줄게 (반말). The redundant causative 연결시켜 드릴게요 is a common over-expansion; 연결하다 already means 'connect,' so 시키다 adds nothing and sounds off to native ears.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '연결해(connect) + 드릴게요(I'll do for you).' The agent promises to route the call through a phone system to a new line or department. The humble 드리다 marks the routing as a service favor. Formal centers use 연결해 드리겠습니다 for an extra tier of formality.
Standard polite in any service or business call. -아 드릴게요 is the baseline. Escalate to 드리겠습니다 for call-center announcements or VIP callers. At home or with peers, 연결해 줄게 is natural.

연결해 드릴게요 routes the call through a phone SYSTEM to another line. 바꿔 드릴게요 hands the SAME handset to a person nearby — a physical swap, not a system transfer. Don't use 연결 for a home hand-off; that sounds comically corporate.

연결해 드릴게요 (standard polite) → 연결해 드리겠습니다 (extra-formal, call-center) → 연결해 줄게 (반말). Adding 바로 before the verb (바로 연결해 드릴게요) signals immediacy. Avoid the redundant causative 연결시켜 드릴게요 — 연결하다 already means 'connect.'
Two traps: (1) Redundant causative 연결시켜 드릴게요 — 연결하다 already means 'connect,' so 시키다 is unnecessary and sounds unnatural. (2) Swapping 연결 for 연락: '나중에 연결드릴게요' is wrong — later contact is 연락, not 연결.

mistakes: Saying 연결시켜 드릴게요. The causative 시키다 is redundant here; 연결하다 already means to connect a call, so the natural form is 연결해 드릴게요.
Confusing 연결 with 연락. 연결 = link two parties right now (transfer); 연락 = contact someone (later). '담당자에게 연락해 주세요' means have them CALL you, not transfer you.
Using 연결해 드릴게요 to hand a phone to a family member. That household hand-off is 바꿔 드릴게요; 연결 implies a technical transfer to another line.

english: They're not available / not in (missed call)
usage: plain polite statement that someone is away
fixed compound noun — the label your phone screen shows
honorific -세요 when the absent person outranks you
examples: A: 박 부장님 계세요? / B: 죄송하지만 지금 부재중이세요. 메모 남겨 드릴까요?
A: Is Manager Park available? / B: I'm sorry, she's out right now. Shall I take a message?
classic office exchange; B uses 부재중이세요 to honor Park, then offers next step
부재중 전화가 세 통이나 와 있네.
Whoa, I've got three missed calls.
통 = counter for calls; -이나 conveys 'as many as three'
담당자가 부재중입니다. 잠시 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
The agent is unavailable. We will contact you again shortly.
formal -입니다 and -겠습니다; the voice-announcement register
nuance: A semi-formal word meaning 'absent from one's seat,' used both to explain someone can't come to the phone and, as the fixed compound 부재중 전화, to label a missed call on your screen. The 한자 roots mark the register: 부재(不在) — 不 'not' + 在 'present/exist' — means 'not present,' while 중(中) means 'in the midst of,' so 부재중 is 'in a state of being absent.' That makes it distinctly more official than everyday 없어요 ('isn't here') or 나갔어요 ('stepped out'), which feel too casual for an office phone. The key synonym contrast: 부재중 means physically AWAY from the phone or desk, while 통화 중 means they ARE at the phone but already speaking to someone else — use the wrong one and you misdirect the caller. Key 변형형: 부재중이에요 (neutral polite) → 부재중이세요 (honorific, about a respected person) → 부재중입니다 (formal announcement) → 부재중 전화 (fixed compound noun for a missed call). Using 부재중 with a close friend who just stepped out would sound oddly stiff; in that case say 잠깐 나갔어요 or 자리 비웠어요.

structuredNuance.t: 부재중 = 不在中, 'in a state of being absent from one's post.' In practice it means: the person is away from their desk or phone right now. As a compound noun, 부재중 전화 is the standard label for a missed call on every Korean smartphone.

Office and phone contexts: 부재중이세요 raises the absent person; 부재중이에요 is neutral. Formal announcements use 부재중입니다. With a friend or in casual speech, 잠깐 나갔어요 or 자리 비웠어요 is more natural — 부재중 sounds stiff in casual situations.
부재중 (away from the phone entirely) vs 통화 중 (at the phone but already on a call). They explain opposite problems. 자리 없어요 / 나갔어요 are the casual near-synonyms for 'stepped out.'

부재중이에요 (neutral polite) → 부재중이세요 (honorific, about someone you respect) → 부재중입니다 (formal announcement register) → 부재중 전화 (compound noun = missed call). The honorific tier is determined entirely by who the absent person is, not who is calling.

Spelling trap: 부재중 is often misspelled as 부제중. The 한자 is 在 (재), meaning 'present,' not 제. 부제 is a totally different word meaning 'subtitle.' Also: using 부재중이에요 in casual conversation sounds oddly formal — stick to 나갔어요 with friends.

mistakes: Pronouncing/spelling it 부제중. It is 부재중 — the 한자 is 在 (재 'present'), not 제. 부제 means a 'subtitle,' a totally different word.
Using it for a friend who just stepped out. 부재중 is office/formal; casually say 잠깐 나갔어요 or 자리 비웠어요.
Confusing 부재중 (away from the phone) with 통화 중 (on another call). They describe opposite reasons someone can't take your call.

english: I'll get in touch with you later
usage: humble promise to reach back out; -드릴게요 raises the listener
I'll reach out in a bit
이따가 = later TODAY (not 나중에, which can be open-ended)
I will get back to you
examples: A: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? / B: 지금 좀 바빠서요. 나중에 연락드릴게요.
A: Is now a good time to talk? / B: I'm a bit busy right now. I'll contact you later.
natural back-and-forth ending a call gracefully; -아서요 trails off to soften
확인하고 나중에 연락드릴게요.
I'll check and get back to you later.
-고 chains 'check first, then contact'
나 지금 운전 중이야. 나중에 연락할게.
I'm driving right now. I'll call you later.
casual; 운전 중 = mid-driving; plain 연락할게, no 드리다
nuance: The polite way to wrap up or postpone a conversation by promising to reach out again — it gracefully ends a call or defers a decision. 연락(連絡) is Sino-Korean: 連 'connect' + 絡 'tie/wrap,' literally 'connecting threads,' and it covers ANY form of contact — call, text, or message — so don't read it as 'phone call only.' The humble 드리다 raises the listener, making -드릴게요 the respectful form; with peers or juniors it relaxes to 연락할게요 / 연락할게. Key 변형형: 나중에 연락드릴게요 (standard) → 이따가 연락드릴게요 (same-day tighter commitment) → 제가 다시 연락드리겠습니다 (formal business) → 나중에 연락할게 (반말). Three contrasts English speakers need: first, 연락 (get in touch later) vs 연결 (transfer a call right now) — never interchangeable; saying 나중에 연결드릴게요 is a clear wiring error. Second, timing words: 나중에 means 'later' with no deadline (could be tomorrow or next week), while 이따가 means 'a bit later TODAY' — promising 이따가 sets a tighter implicit commitment. Third, register: 드리다 honors the listener, so using 연락드릴게요 toward someone clearly junior to you can sound over-deferential; plain 연락할게요 is more natural then.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '나중에(later) + 연락(contact) + 드릴게요(I'll do for you).' A humble promise to reach back out by ANY channel — call, text, or message — at a future time. Used to close a call gracefully or defer an answer.

Said when ending a call because you're busy, need to check something, or simply can't talk now. -드릴게요 is the respectful form for seniors and clients. With peers or juniors, 연락할게요 / 연락할게 is natural and avoids sounding over-deferential.

연락 (get in touch later) vs 연결 (connect / transfer a call right now): never swap them. 나중에 (unspecified future) vs 이따가 (later today): 이따가 implies a tighter same-day commitment. Both pairs carry real social weight.
나중에 연락드릴게요 (standard) → 이따가 연락드릴게요 (tighter, same-day) → 제가 다시 연락드리겠습니다 (formal business) → 나중에 연락할게요 (neutral, no 드리다) → 나중에 연락할게 (반말). The humble 드리다 is the only element that shifts with register.

Two traps: (1) Using 드릴게요 with a junior — it over-honors them; use plain 연락할게요 instead. (2) Swapping 연락 for 연결: '나중에 연결드릴게요' sounds like 'I'll transfer your call later,' which makes no sense — later contact is 연락, not 연결.

mistakes: Reading 연락 as 'phone call' only. 연락 = contact by any channel (call OR text). '연락 주세요' means 'get in touch,' not specifically 'phone me.'
Swapping in 연결 for 연락. 나중에 연결드릴게요 is wrong — 연결 is connecting a call now; later contact is 연락.
Using 드릴게요 to someone clearly below you in status. The humble 드리다 raises the listener; with a junior, plain 연락할게요 sounds more natural than over-deferential 연락드릴게요.

english: I'll put them on / pass you over (to another person)
usage: I'll put them on the line
humble; handing the SAME phone to the person you want
One moment, I'll pass you over
잠시만요 buys the beat while you fetch them
I'll put the person in charge on
examples: A: 아버지 계세요? / B: 네, 잠시만요. 바꿔 드릴게요.
A: Is your father there? / B: Yes, one moment. I'll put him on.
typical home call hand-off; B confirms presence, then offers to pass the phone
제가 잘 몰라서요. 아는 사람으로 바꿔 드릴게요.
I'm not sure, so I'll put on someone who knows.
-으로 marks who you're swapping TO; reason given first with -아서요
엄마 찾아? 잠깐만, 바꿔 줄게.
Looking for Mom? Hold on, I'll put her on.
casual at home; 줄게 not 드릴게요
nuance: Used when the person who answered hands the physical receiver (or the call) to the person the caller actually wants. The verb is 바꾸다, literally 'to change or swap,' which on the phone idiomatically means swapping who is speaking — you are not changing any object; you are exchanging voices on the line. The humble -아 드리다 makes it a service favor; 바꿔 줄게 is the peer/home version with plain 주다. The single most critical contrast is 바꾸다 vs 연결하다: 바꿔 드릴게요 is for physically handing the same device to a person standing right there (a colleague, a family member), while 연결해 드릴게요 is a system-level transfer to a different line or extension that you cannot simply hand-deliver. Using 연결 at home to hand mom the phone sounds comically corporate; using 바꾸다 for a multi-department transfer in an office sounds naively low-tech. The irregular conjugation trips learners: the stem is 바꾸-, and 바꾸- + -어 contracts cleanly to 바꿔, not 바껴 (which would falsely imply a stem 바끼-).

structuredNuance.t: Literally '바꿔(swap) + 드릴게요(I'll do for you).' Handing the phone to the person you want — swapping who speaks, not transferring through a system. The 바꾸다 in phone context always means this person-to-person voice exchange.
Home and office. Keep 드릴게요 (humble 드리다) with customers, seniors, or anyone you'd 존댓말. 바꿔 드리겠습니다 is the formal call-center equivalent. At home with peers, 바꿔 줄게 is natural.

바꿔 드릴게요 = hand the SAME phone to a person physically nearby (home or small office). 연결해 드릴게요 = route the call through a phone SYSTEM to a different line or department. They are different mechanical acts; swapping them sounds wrong in both directions.
바꾸다 → 바꿔 (바꾸 + 어) → 바꿔 드릴게요 (humble) / 바꿔 드리겠습니다 (formal) / 바꿔 줄게 (반말). Stronger form: 잠시만요, 바로 바꿔 드릴게요 (right away).

Conjugation error: the stem is 바꾸-, so 바꾸 + 어 = 바꿔, NOT 바껴. 바껴 implies a non-existent stem 바끼-. Also: using 연결해 드릴게요 when you mean 바꿔 드릴게요 — they are not synonyms; one is a physical hand-off, the other a system transfer.

mistakes: Using 연결해 드릴게요 to hand the phone to a family member. At home it's 바꿔 드릴게요; 연결 implies a technical transfer to another line, not passing the same handset.
Writing 바꿔 as 바껴. The stem is 바꾸- (바꾸 + 어 = 바꿔). 바껴 wrongly assumes a stem 바끼-, which does not exist.
Confusing 바꾸다 (swap/change) with 바라다 (hope) or 비꾸다 (no such word). On the phone, 'put someone on' is strictly 바꾸다 → 바꿔.

usage: polite, said TO the caller; 거셨어요 = honorific past of 걸다
I think you have the wrong number
-것 같다 hedges so you don't sound blunt
There's no one by that name here
the usual follow-up; -는데요 trails off softly
반말 — typically the CALLER admitting it
examples: A: 거기 서울 치과 아닌가요? / B: 아닌데요. 전화 잘못 거신 것 같은데요.
A: Isn't this Seoul Dental? / B: No, it isn't. I think you may have the wrong number.
A/B exchange; B uses the softened -신 것 같은데요 to avoid sounding blunt while correcting the caller
죄송하지만 전화 잘못 거셨어요. 그런 분 안 계세요.
Sorry, but you've got the wrong number — no one by that name here.
죄송하지만 cushions the correction; 그런 분 안 계세요 = honorific 'no such person is here'
어? 미안, 내가 전화 잘못 걸었어.
Huh? Sorry, I dialed the wrong number.
the caller owning the mistake; 내가 + 걸었어 — subject shifts to I, no honorific needed
nuance: What you say when a stranger has reached you by mistake. The verb is 걸다, the standard Korean verb for placing a call (전화를 걸다, literally 'hook up / hang a call'), and here it appears as the honorific past 거셨어요, so you are politely informing the CALLER that they dialed wrong — note you still raise them with -시- even while delivering bad news. When the CALLER realizes the mistake and apologizes, they own it as 제가 잘못 걸었어요 ('I misdialed'), so subject determines verb form: 거셨어요 (you did) vs 걸었어요 (I did). To soften an awkward correction, Koreans add a hedge: 잘못 거신 것 같은데요 ('it seems you may have the wrong number') is far gentler than the bare statement. The headline English-speaker trap is the irregular conjugation: 걸다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb — before honorific -시-, the ㄹ drops, giving 거시- → 거셨어요, not the over-regularized 걸으셨어요. A second near-synonym follow-up line is 여기 그런 분 안 계세요 ('there is no such person here'), which provides the evidence behind the wrong-number claim.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '전화(call) + 잘못(wrongly) + 거셨어요(you placed).' Notifies a caller they've reached the wrong number. Despite correcting them, the honorific -시- remains because Korean politeness is independent of the message content. Softened version: 잘못 거신 것 같은데요 ('it seems you may have the wrong number').

Said by the person who received the mistaken call. Standard polite -세요 / -셨어요 with any stranger. The caller admitting the error uses plain past 잘못 걸었어요 (polite) or 잘못 걸었어 (반말). 죄송하지만 as a lead-in is a natural cushion before correcting.

여기 그런 분 안 계세요 ('there's no such person here') is the natural follow-up line rather than a synonym — it gives the concrete evidence for the wrong-number claim. 잘못 거신 것 같은데요 is the hedged, softer alternative to the direct 잘못 거셨어요.
걸다 → 거셨어요 (you, honorific past) / 걸었어요 (I, plain past) / 거신 것 같은데요 (hedged). Caller admitting it: 제가 잘못 걸었어요. The ㄹ-drop before -시- is the key irregular to master.
Over-regularizing the ㄹ-irregular: 걸다 drops the ㄹ before -시-, so the honorific past is 거셨어요, NOT 걸으셨어요. 걸으셨어요 is a beginner error that sounds like you are conjugating 걷다 (to walk) instead.

mistakes: Saying 전화 잘못 걸으셨어요. 걸다 is a ㄹ-irregular: the ㄹ drops before -시-, giving 거셨어요. 걸으셨어요 over-regularizes the stem.
Using 거셨어요 about yourself. When YOU misdial, the subject is 제가, so say 제가 잘못 걸었어요 — keep the honorific -시- only for the other person.
Mixing 걸다 (place a call) with 받다 (answer a call). You 전화를 걸다 to dial and 전화를 받다 to pick up; 'wrong number' is about 걸다, the dialing.

english: Please call back in a little while
usage: asks the caller to retry later rather than wait on hold
Call back in a bit, please
조금 이따 = casual 'in a little bit'
examples: A: 지금 연결이 어렵나요? / B: 회의 중이라서요. 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요.
A: Is it hard to connect right now? / B: I'm in a meeting. Please call back in a little while.
A/B exchange; B gives reason with -이라서요 then makes the callback request
통화량이 많습니다. 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요.
Call volume is high. Please call again shortly.
the exact wording of an automated busy-line announcement — recognizing this saves frustration
나 밥 먹고 있어. 이따 다시 걸어.
I'm eating. Call me back later.
casual; -고 있어 = in the middle of; 이따 pins it to today
nuance: A polite request for the caller to try again soon instead of holding the line. It breaks into 잠시 후에 ('after a short while': 잠시 from 한자 暫時 'brief time,' + 후 後 'after' + -에 locative) and 다시 걸어 주세요 ('please dial again'), where 걸다 is the verb for placing a call and 주세요 frames the redial as a favor you are requesting. This phrase is verbatim the wording of Korean automated busy-line recordings, so recognizing it in the wild is as useful as producing it yourself. Key 변형형: 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요 (standard) → 잠시 후 다시 걸어 주시겠어요? (extra-polite) → 이따 다시 걸어 주세요 (casual/same-day) → 이따 다시 걸어 (반말). Two English-speaker voice traps: first, 'call back' is the ACTIVE verb 걸다 → 걸어 주세요, NOT the passive 걸리다 (걸려 주세요 is wrong because 걸리다 means 'be caught/take time'); second, don't confuse 잠시 후에 ('after a moment' — telling someone to ACT later) with 잠시만요 ('hold on just a sec' — telling someone to STAY put now); they give opposite instructions.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '잠시 후에(after a short while) + 다시(again) + 걸어 주세요(please dial).' Sends the caller away to retry rather than holding. This is the exact wording of Korean automated busy-line announcements — recognizing it in the wild matters as much as saying it yourself.

Said when you cannot take the call now — in a meeting, on another call, in a noisy place. Standard polite 주세요 suits any situation. 주시겠어요? softens it further for a VIP or formal context. 이따 다시 걸어 is the casual peer/반말 version.

잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요 = call back after a moment (future action). 잠시만요 = wait/stay on the line for a second (present freeze). They give opposite directions to the caller — one sends them away, the other holds them in place. 이따 다시 전화 주세요 is the colloquial near-synonym.

잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요 (standard polite) → 잠시 후 다시 걸어 주시겠어요? (extra-polite) → 이따 다시 걸어 주세요 (casual, same-day) → 이따 다시 걸어 (반말). The active stem 걸- (걸어 주세요) must not be confused with passive 걸리- (걸려요 = 'it takes time').

잠시(暫時): 暫 'brief/for now' + 時 'time' = 'a brief time.' 후(後) = 'after/behind.' Together 잠시 후에 = 'after a brief period.' The 한자 origin explains why this phrase sounds formal and fits automated announcements.

Voice confusion: 'call back' is ACTIVE 걸다 → 걸어 주세요; the passive form is 걸리다 (걸려 주세요 = 'please be caught/take time'), which makes no sense as a callback request. Also: 잠시 후에 ≠ 잠시만요 — one dismisses, the other freezes. Using the wrong one creates confusion about what the caller should do.

mistakes: Saying 다시 걸려 주세요. The active verb is 걸다 (걸어 주세요 = 'please dial'). 걸리다 is passive ('be caught / take time'), so 걸려 주세요 is wrong here.
Confusing 잠시 후에 with 잠시만요. 잠시 후에 = 'after a short while' (go retry later); 잠시만요 = 'hold on a second' (stay put now). Opposite instructions.
Treating 잠시 후 and 잠깐 as fully interchangeable in formal speech. 잠시 후(에) is the standard announcement register; 잠깐만 is more casual and odd in an automated message.

english: The signal is weak / poor reception
usage: states the reception problem; 신호 takes -가 as subject
It's because reception is weak here
-아서요 trails off, giving the reason a call dropped
I can't get a good signal
잡히다 = the signal is 'caught'/picked up; very natural alt
examples: A: 여보세요? 목소리가 자꾸 끊겨요. / B: 여기 신호가 약해서요. 이따 다시 걸게요.
A: Hello? Your voice keeps cutting out. / B: The signal's weak here. I'll call you back in a bit.
A/B troubleshoot exchange; A names the symptom, B gives the cause and proposes the fix
지하라서 신호가 약해요. 끊고 다시 걸게요.
I'm underground so the signal's weak. Let me hang up and call back.
-라서 reason; 끊고 다시 = hang up then redial — the natural fix sequence
산속이라 신호 약해. 이따 통화하자.
I'm in the mountains, signal's weak. Let's talk later.
casual; -자 = let's; 통화하자 = let's talk by phone; 이따 = later today
nuance: The natural way to explain why a call sounds garbled or keeps dropping: the cellular 신호 is 약하다 ('weak'). 신호(信號) is Sino-Korean: 信 'trust/sign' + 號 'mark/number,' literally a 'signal mark,' covering signals broadly — traffic lights are also 신호등 ('signal lamp') — so context tells you it means cell reception here. The key near-synonym is 신호가 잘 안 잡혀요 ('the signal isn't being picked up well'), which uses the passive 잡히다 ('be caught') and is equally natural; in Korea people alternate freely between the two. Key 변형형: 신호가 약해요 (standard) → 신호가 잘 안 잡혀요 (passive alternative, equally common) → 여기 신호가 약해서요 (reason-trailing form) → 신호 약해 (반말). Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, reaching for the loanword 사인 — in Korean, 사인 means a 'signature' or a gestured 'sign,' not cell reception; phone signal is 신호. Second, the adjective choice: signal strength pairs with 약하다/세다 (weak/strong), not 작다/크다 (small/big) — saying 신호가 작아요 sounds wrong the way 'the signal is small' does in English. Pair the signal complaint with 잘 안 들려요 ('I can't hear well') to explain to the other person WHY you keep saying 뭐라고요?

structuredNuance.t: 신호 = cell signal/reception; 약해요 = is weak. Together: 'the reception is poor.' Pair it with 잘 안 들려요 ('I can't hear well') to link the cause (weak signal) to the effect (garbled audio). Used whenever a call sounds broken, drops, or gets patchy.

Said mid-call to explain audio problems. Polite 약해요 suits any phone situation. Casual 신호 약해 (particle dropped, plain stem) is natural with friends. 신호가 약해서요 with a trailing -아서요 works as a soft apology-reason.

신호가 잘 안 잡혀요 ('the signal isn't being picked up') uses passive 잡히다 and is equally common — alternate freely. 신호가 약해요 emphasizes strength; 안 잡혀요 emphasizes availability/presence. Both explain the same situation.

신호가 약해요 (standard) → 신호가 잘 안 잡혀요 (passive, equally natural) → 여기 신호가 약해서요 (reason-trailing) → 신호 약해 (반말). Opposites: 신호가 세요/강해요 (strong signal). The passive 잡히다 pairs only with 잘 안: '신호 안 잡혀요' or '신호가 잘 안 잡혀요.'

Two mistakes: (1) Using 사인 for 'signal' — 사인 in Korean means a signature or a gestured sign, NOT cell reception; the phone word is 신호. (2) Wrong adjective scale — signal strength is 약하다/세다 (weak/strong), not 작다/크다 (small/big); '신호가 작아요' sounds unnatural.

mistakes: Using 사인 for 'signal.' Cell reception is 신호; 사인 in Korean means a signature or a hand sign, so '사인이 약해요' is wrong.
Saying 신호가 작아요/커요. Strength pairs with 약하다/세다 (weak/strong), not 작다/크다 (small/big). '신호가 세요' = 'the signal is strong.'
Confusing 신호 with 신호등. Bare 신호 on the phone = reception/signal; 신호등 specifically is a traffic light. Don't add 등 when talking about a call.

usage: Can you hear me all right?
honorific check on the OTHER side mid-call; subject is them
Can you hear my voice clearly?
제 목소리 spells out exactly what they should be hearing
지금은 = 'now (as opposed to before)'; after fixing reception
examples: A: 여보세요? 잘 들리세요? / B: 네, 잘 들려요. 말씀하세요.
A: Hello? Can you hear me okay? / B: Yes, I can hear you fine. Go ahead.
opening audio check and clearance; B gives a green light with 말씀하세요
여기로 옮겼는데 지금은 잘 들리세요?
I moved over here — is it clear now?
-는데 sets the context change; 지금은 contrasts with the earlier bad audio
야, 잘 들려? 자꾸 끊기는 것 같은데.
Hey, can you hear me? It keeps cutting out.
casual; 끊기다 = (the call) keeps dropping; -는 것 같은데 = seems like
nuance: The flip side of reporting 잘 안 들려요 ('I can't hear well'): instead of describing your own trouble, you ask whether the OTHER person can hear YOU, which is why it is phrased from their perspective. The grammar hinge is voice: 들리다 is the intransitive/passive 'to be heard, to be audible' — something reaches the ear on its own — so 잘 들리세요? literally asks 'is it being heard well by you?' The honorific -세요 raises the listener without changing the meaning. On video calls, Zoom, and Google Meet, the same 들리세요? is the universal audio-check opening, so mastering it pays dividends far beyond phone calls. The critical English-speaker error is swapping in 듣다, the transitive 'to listen' that takes an object: 잘 듣고 있어요? means 'are you listening (paying attention)?' — a scolding, not a reception check. A second look-alike hazard is 들리다 (be audible) vs 들다 (lift/hold; cost; enter): completely different verbs that happen to share a root surface. Natural adverb partners are 잘 (well), 안 (not), and 잘 안 together for the soft negative.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '잘(well) + 들리세요?(is it being heard by you)?' — asking if the audio is reaching the OTHER person clearly. 들리다 is passive/intransitive: the sound comes to the ear; you are not asking them to try harder. Used on any voice channel: phone, video call, speakerphone.

Said at the start of a call, after moving to a new location, or any time audio seems shaky. -세요 is the polite honorific form. 잘 들려요? is neutral polite (no subject honorific); 잘 들려? is 반말. On video calls this is the universal opening audio check.
잘 들리세요? (can YOU hear me?) vs 잘 들려요 / 잘 안 들려요 (I can / can't hear). The subject flips direction. 제 목소리 잘 들리세요? is more precise when there is a specific sound (your voice) to check.
들리다 conjugates: 들리세요? (honorific) / 들려요? (polite, no subject honor) / 들려? (반말). The passive stem 들리- is fixed; adverbs 잘 and 안 slot directly before it.

Critical swap: 잘 듣고 있어요? uses 듣다 (transitive 'to listen/pay attention') and sounds accusatory — 'are you paying attention?' The audio check must use 들리다 (intransitive, passive 'be audible'): 잘 들리세요?. Also: 들리다 (be audible) vs 들다 (lift/cost/enter) — same root surface, completely different verbs.

mistakes: Saying 잘 듣고 있어요? to mean 'can you hear me.' That asks 'are you listening (paying attention)?' and sounds accusatory. The reception check is 잘 들리세요? with 들리다.
Confusing 들리다 (be audible) with 들다 (lift / cost / enter). Same-looking roots, unrelated meanings; the hearing verb is 들리다 → 들려요/들리세요.
Treating 들리다 as transitive with an object + 를. It's intransitive: the thing heard takes -가/-이 (제 목소리가 잘 들려요), not 제 목소리를 들려요.

english: They're on another call right now
usage: They're on the phone right now
honorific -세요 about the person the caller wants
The line's busy / on a call
plain polite, about a line or neutral subject
I'm on the phone right now
examples: A: 이 과장님 연결해 주세요. / B: 지금 통화 중이세요. 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주시겠어요?
A: Please connect me to Manager Lee. / B: He's on another call right now. Could you call back shortly?
classic busy-line exchange; B raises Lee with -세요 then offers a polite callback request
몇 번을 걸어도 계속 통화 중이네요.
No matter how many times I call, the line's still busy.
-아도 = 'even if'; 계속 = keeps; -네요 = the caller's frustrated observation
미안, 나 지금 통화 중이야. 이따 연락할게.
Sorry, I'm on the phone. I'll get back to you.
casual; speaker about THEMSELVES — plain -이야, no -세요; 이따 = later today
nuance: Explains that a person's line is occupied because they are already in conversation with someone else. 통화 중 = 'in the middle of a call': 통화(通話) is 'a connected voice conversation' (通 'connect' + 話 'speech'), and 중(中) is the 한자 suffix meaning 'in the midst of' — the same 중 you see in 회의 중 ('in a meeting'), 식사 중 ('in the middle of eating'), and 운전 중 ('mid-driving'), making this a productive pattern. The honorific is the subtle part: add -세요 only when speaking ABOUT a person you respect (부장님 통화 중이세요), keep plain 통화 중이에요 about a line or a neutral party, and say 통화 중이야 about yourself in casual speech — crucially, never use -세요 about yourself (저 통화 중이세요 wrongly honors yourself). The essential contrast is 통화 중 vs 부재중: 통화 중 means they ARE at the phone but already speaking to someone, while 부재중 means they are AWAY from it entirely — opposite problems that send the caller in opposite directions. A natural collocation is 계속 통화 중이에요 ('keeps being busy') for repeated failed attempts.

structuredNuance.t: 통화 중 = 'in the middle of a phone conversation.' The line is occupied because the person is already speaking — they are PRESENT but unavailable. 중(中) is a productive 한자 suffix: 회의 중 (in a meeting), 식사 중 (eating), 운전 중 (driving). Knowing the pattern unlocks many parallel phrases.

말하는 상황: someone calls but the target is already on another call. -세요 is added only when the person you are describing outranks you (부장님 통화 중이세요). Plain 통화 중이에요 for a neutral line. For yourself: 통화 중이에요 (polite) or 통화 중이야 (반말). NEVER 저 통화 중이세요.

통화 중 (at the phone, already talking to someone) vs 부재중 (away from the phone entirely). These are opposite reasons for unavailability and must not be swapped — one means the person is present but busy; the other means they are gone.

통화(通話): 通 'connect' + 話 'speech' = a live connected conversation. 중(中) = 'in the midst of.' The compound 통화 중 = 'in the midst of a connected conversation.' The same 중 suffix works with any ongoing activity noun.

Honorific self-reference error: never say 저 통화 중이세요 — -세요 raises the SUBJECT, and you never honor yourself. A second error: using 통화 중 when you mean 부재중, or vice versa — they give callers opposite information about where the person is.

mistakes: Adding -세요 about your own call. For yourself say 통화 중이에요 / 통화 중이야; 저 통화 중이세요 wrongly honors yourself.
Confusing 통화 중 (on another call) with 부재중 (away/absent). They are opposite reasons someone can't take your call — 통화 중 = present but talking.
Saying 통화하고 있으세요? as the busy-signal explanation. To report the busy line you state 통화 중이세요; 통화하고 계세요? is a question, not the status label.
